title: Fractional Experts: ¿Cuál es su rol y por qué son necesarios?
summary: Los fractional experts permiten a las empresas a acceder a conocimiento especializado. En este artículo explicamos más sobre los detalles de este nuevo rol.
body_text: El trabajo remoto no sólo está facilitando la contratación de trabajadores de otros países sino también promueve la evolución de la forma de trabajo de como la conocíamos. Este es el caso específico de los fractional experts, quienes han surgido ante la demanda de expertos que sean capaz de crear estrategias y llevarlas a cabo pero sin tener que realizar una contratación full-time, lo que le brinda ventajas a ambas partes. ¿Qué es un fractional expert? ‍ También conocido como fractional advisors, estos son líderes dentro de start-ups, o en empresas que oscilan entre los 100 y 500 colaboradores (aunque también pueden presentarse en organizaciones de diferente tamaño o estructura). ‍ Como su nombre lo dice, estos solo dan una “fracción” de su tiempo y recursos para un proyecto. A diferencia de un empleado de tiempo completo, el cual debe de cumplir con un número de horas y seguir los lineamientos de la empresa respecto a los horarios y lugares de trabajo. ‍ Pero a los fractional experts tampoco se les puede considerar o llamar colaboradores de tiempo parcial o medio tiempo ya que el impacto que su expertise tiene en el negocio, se mide más allá del tiempo que aporta en la empresa y suele recaer en valor, impacto o resultados. ‍ Estos expertos pueden ocupar posiciones clave de liderazgo debido a su experiencia y a su vez, apoyar a las empresas cuando estas se encuentran a punto de lanzar una iniciativa (nuevo mercado, tecnología, tipo de producto, entre otros). ‍ Es importante hacer la distinción entre un consultor y un fractional expert. El primero se centra en evaluar la situación y un problema en específico que tiene la empresa. Una vez concluido su análisis, emite recomendaciones o pasos a seguir que la compañía puede implementar para lograr su propósito. Pero, el papel que juega el segundo va más allá de sugerencias para lograr resultados. Este también forma parte del proceso de ejecución de las nuevas medidas y se involucra en hacerle frente a posibles retos que surjan durante ese proceso. ‍ Por otro lado, un fractional expert tampoco es un freelancer ya que estos solo se enfocan en llevar a cabo una sola tarea gracias a su experiencia y nivel de habilidades pero no se les considera al momento de desarrollar las estrategias que pueden ayudar a una empresa a cumplir sus objetivos. ‍ En resumen, estas son las tareas de las que un fractional expert puede encargarse: Combinar conocimiento (al igual que un consultor), con experiencia y habilidades. Ejercer un puesto clave dentro de un equipo, ya que puede asesorar estratégicamente y ejecutar al mismo tiempo. Es decir que no se limita a hacer recomendaciones ni a trabajar en una sola tarea. Apoyar en un proyecto para lograr el cumplimiento de los objetivos y generar resultados para el negocio. Desempeñarse en un rol estratégico o de ejecución, esto dependerá de las preferencias de los directivos de la empresa o de las necesidades del proyecto. ¿Cuándo contratar a un fractional expert? El trabajo on-demand ya no es un concepto del futuro, sino que se trata de una realidad que cada día esta más presente. Con la situación económica actual, el aumento de profesionales y de expertos libres de contrato y la cautela de las empresas a realizar grandes inversiones; los fractional experts parecen ser el paso natural tanto para expertos como para las compañías. ‍ Además, en aquellos casos en los que una sola persona tiene varias funciones dentro de una organización (como los CEO’s de startups), es probable que estos necesiten de la ayuda de un fractional expert que les permita enfocarse en lo importante. ‍ Por otro lado, los fractional experts son perfectos para aquellos proyectos que requieren expertise y conocimientos específicos sobre un área pero que no necesariamente van a necesitar esa posición para el largo plazo. Si la empresa está en desarrollo de un nuevo producto o feature que atacará a una nicho determinado, lo mejor será contratar a un experto que pueda brindar su conocimiento de dicho target durante el período de desarrollo y lanzamiento. ‍ En caso de que la compañía pueda pagar el costo de un fractional expert que se encargue de crear el plan y desarrollar un proyecto, entonces se debería considerar la posibilidad de contratar a una de estas figuras. ‍ Los fractional experts también pueden apoyar a la empresa en diferentes formas. Te presentamos tan solo algunos ejemplos: Brindar soporte interno, ya que ayudan a que los puestos ejecutivos tengan menos responsabilidades en sus manos y les permite centrarse en los asuntos importantes de la empresa. Ofrecer liderazgo para proyectos internos que no están relacionados con el producto o servicio y que impactan a la organización desde adentro. Tal puede ser el caso de nuevos planes en el área de Recursos Humanos o Finanzas. Funcionar como un período de espera para una contratación en el largo plazo. Si dentro de los planes de la empresa se encuentra la incorporación de un experto full time pero no de forma inmediata; un fractional expert podría apoyar a ocupar esa posición y tomar las riendas del proyecto o equipo en cuestión. ‍ Ventajas de un fractional expert ‍ Estos roles son una buena opción cuando se necesita que los proyectos avancen rápidamente y que estos generen resultados, sin necesariamente invertir en todos los recursos relacionados a una contratación de tiempo completo. ‍ A través de la contratación de un fractional expert, las empresas tienen la oportunidad de optimizar recursos al no tener que desembolsar una gran cantidad de dinero en la incorporación de un ejecutivo de alto nivel para el largo plazo. ‍ Para los expertos, esta modalidad de contratación les beneficia ya que pueden mantener su autonomía al mismo tiempo que cuentan con un ingreso estable por un tiempo determinado. ‍ En resumen, este modelo ayuda a las empresas por las siguientes razones: Les brinda acceso a un talento específico con conocimientos, habilidades y background específico que puede apoyarlos con un proyecto definido. Apoya a romper la barrera mental del miedo a un despido masivo (por parte de los nuevos colaboradores). A reducir costos, ya que es necesario pagar prestaciones como si fuera un empleado de tiempo completo. ‍ Mientras que para los fractional experts, esta “modalidad” les beneficia al: Crear diferentes fuentes de ingreso, lo que reduce la posibilidad de un impacto económico negativo por despido. Ofrecerles mayor flexibilidad al elegir el tipo de proyecto con el que se pueden involucrar y los horarios de trabajo. Brindarles un aprendizaje exponencial al participar en diferentes industrias y en varios tipos de compañías. Generar mejores ingresos al cotizar bajo expertise y no como forma de compensación. ‍ La demanda por los fractional experts ha ido en aumento en los últimos años, tanto que ya existen compañías que han aprovechado esta oportunidad para atacar las necesidades del mercado y enfocarse en la búsqueda de dichos perfiles. ‍ La posición de fractional expert se ha vuelto relevante y empresas como A-Team (especializada en product designers) atiende estas necesidades. De esta forma, la compañía logró un crecimiento de 7x durante el 2021 y un financiamiento de 60 millones de USD. ‍ Otra prueba de su relevancia es el surgimiento de comunidades como The Fractional Expert , la cual funciona como un marketplace en el que los profesionales. ofrecen sus servicios y las empresas los contratan. ‍ Si estás desarrollando un proyecto nuevo y necesites la voz de un especialista, tal vez sea buena idea contratar a un fractional expert. ‍

title: 🚩 Red Flag | Expat Edition | TaxGPT's Newsletter
summary: Tax Responsibilities for U.S. Citizens and Resident Aliens Living Abroad: Filing Requirements, Exclusions, Credits, and Avoiding Double Taxation
body_text: FATCA and FBAR Reporting Obligations ‍ As a US expatriate, you may also be subject to additional reporting requirements related to your foreign financial accounts and assets. These requirements are governed by the Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA) and the Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts (FBAR) regulations. ‍ FATCA Reporting ‍ FATCA requires US taxpayers, including expatriates, to report certain foreign financial assets on Form 8938 if the total value of those assets exceeds specified thresholds. The thresholds vary based on your filing status and whether you live inside or outside the United States. ‍ For the 2024 tax year, the reporting thresholds for US expatriates are: ‍ - Unmarried taxpayers living abroad: $200,000 on the last day of the tax year or $300,000 at any time during the year - Married taxpayers filing jointly and living abroad: $400,000 on the last day of the tax year or $600,000 at any time during the year ‍ Failure to comply with FATCA reporting requirements can result in significant penalties, including a $10,000 penalty for failure to file Form 8938 and an additional $50,000 penalty for continued failure to file after IRS notification. ‍ FBAR Reporting ‍ The FBAR (FinCEN Form 114) is a separate reporting requirement for US persons, including expatriates, who have an interest in or signature authority over foreign financial accounts with an aggregate value exceeding $10,000 at any time during the calendar year. ‍ The FBAR is filed electronically with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), a bureau of the US Department of the Treasury, and is due by April 15th of each year (with an automatic extension to October 15th if you live abroad). ‍ Failure to file the FBAR can result in severe civil and criminal penalties, including a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per violation for non-willful violations and up to 50% of the account balance for willful violations. ‍ State Tax Requirements for US Expatriates ‍ While the focus is often on federal tax obligations, it's important for US expatriates to also consider their potential state tax requirements. Some states may still require you to file a state income tax return, even if you live and work abroad, depending on factors such as your domicile or residency status. ‍ For example, if you maintain a permanent place of abode in a particular state or spend a significant amount of time there, you may be considered a resident for state tax purposes and be required to file a state income tax return and pay state taxes on your worldwide income. For instance: Alabama, California, Hawaii, Massachusetts, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania do not have a FEIE. ‍ Additionally, some states may tax certain types of income earned by non-residents, such as rental income from property located within the state or income from businesses operating in the state. ‍ It's crucial for US expatriates to understand their specific state tax obligations and file accordingly to avoid potential penalties and interest charges. Consulting with a tax professional familiar with state tax laws can help ensure compliance and minimize your overall tax burden. ‍ In conclusion , navigating the complex tax landscape as a US expatriate requires a thorough understanding of various concepts and reporting requirements. By familiarizing yourself with the principles of worldwide income taxation, the FEIE and FTC, FATCA and FBAR reporting, and potential state tax obligations, you can better manage your tax responsibilities and avoid costly penalties. Seeking guidance from a qualified tax professional with expertise in expatriate taxation can further ensure compliance and help you maximize your tax benefits. ‍ For additional information regarding taxes for expats: https://www.irs.gov/publications/p54 https://www.irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/foreign-earned-income-exclusion https://www.irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/foreign-tax-credit https://www.irs.gov/businesses/corporations/foreign-account-tax-compliance-act-fatca https://www.fincen.gov/report-foreign-bank-and-financial-accounts ‍

title: Vial Optimization & JW Modifier: Cut Drug Waste and Denials
summary: Trellis AI | Streamline Your Pre-Service Operations
body_text: High-cost infusions often come in fixed vial sizes, so vial optimization is key to minimizing drug waste and related denials. Vial optimization (VSO) means selecting the combination of vial sizes that yields the least leftover volume. For example, if a patient needs 150 mg and the drug comes in 50 mg or 100 mg vials, using three 50 mg vials (total 150 mg) avoids having to open two 100 mg vials and wasting 50 mg. In fact, payers are increasingly mandating vial size optimization – Medicare will not reimburse waste beyond what would remain if the provider used the smallest necessary vial combination. The Center for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) encourages providers to administer drugs “in such a way that these are used most efficiently, in a clinically appropriate manner.” Even with optimization, some waste from single-use vials is inevitable. That’s where the JW modifier comes in. The JW modifier is used on claims to indicate the amount of drug discarded (not administered) from a single-dose vial . To bill for discarded medication, document the exact wasted amount in the chart and append JW on a separate claim line with the number of units wasted. For example, if a 100 mg vial is opened but only 90 mg given, 10 mg is wasted – bill one line for the dose and another with JW for the waste (assuming the HCPCS code unit is 10 mg). Do not use JW for multi-dose vials or for waste within a single HCPCS billing unit (if you already rounded up). As of July 2023, Medicare also requires the JZ modifier when no drug is wasted from a single-use vial. This means every single-dose vial drug line must have either JW (if there was discard) or JZ (if none) to be accepted. Implementing these practices not only captures revenue that would be lost as uncompensated waste, but also avoids denials. Medicare will reject claims lacking JW/JZ as unprocessable . Likewise, some payers limit waste payment to what’s reasonable – if you could have used smaller vials, extra waste may be non-reimbursable. By scheduling patients strategically and adhering to vial size guidance, infusion centers can keep waste minimal. When waste does occur, proper use of JW with clear documentation (“discarded 5 mg, drawn up and not used”) ensures you get paid for that drug instead of absorbing the cost. Payers want assurance that discarded medication was truly unavoidable and properly reported. Through vial optimization and diligent use of JW/JZ modifiers, infusion providers can cut drug waste and related denials , turning what was once lost cost into recoverable revenue.

TAMPA, FL (November 2024) – Kforce is proud to continue its third annual Season of Impact, a stewardship initiative encouraging employees to make a difference during the fall and winter months. The philanthropic effort is an evolution of the firm’s Day of Giving, which started in 2016. This year, Kforce is placing a special emphasis on aiding those impacted by hurricanes Helene and Milton. The back-to-back storms devastated Tampa Bay, where nearly a third of the firm’s employees live. North Carolina and other parts of the coast also face long recoveries. In continuation of the long-standing relationship with Feeding Tampa Bay (a Kforce corporate-sponsored charity ), the firm will donate 1.6 million meals to address food insecurity in the aftermath of the storm. Local employees will also participate in a “warehouse takeover,” packing meals for the community. Additional donations will be made to MANNA Food Bank in North Carolina, Hope Children’s Home and Fezziwig – a Tampa-based nonprofit offering assistance to charitable organizations and individuals in crisis. “These donations are one step in an ongoing effort to support our people and our communities,” CEO and President Joe Liberatore said. “We are proud of the culture our leaders and associates have built – one of charity, goodwill and compassion. Kforcers across the nation are encouraged to support causes they are passionate about – whether with their time, talent or treasure. In the past, Kforcers have packed hygiene and home supplies for those in need, cared for shelter animals, volunteered at local schools, organized food drives and wrapped holiday gifts. “Community stewardship is a foundational tenant of Kforce culture – it’s who we are,” Chief Experience Officer Andy Thomas said. “While our teams give back to their communities year-round, the Season of Impact creates a focused effort to maximize our contributions during a meaningful time.” About Kforce Kforce is a solutions firm specializing in technology, finance and accounting, and professional staffing services. title: Jet Admin vs Retool: Which Low-Code Platform Is Better for Your Business Apps?
summary: If you're evaluating low-code platforms for building internal tools, customer portals, or admin panels, Jet Admin vs Retool is likely at the top of your shortlist. Both platforms let you connect to data sources and ship custom business apps fast-but they're built for fundamentally different teams and use cases. Jet
body_text: If you're evaluating low-code platforms for building internal tools, customer portals, or admin panels, Jet Admin vs Retool is likely at the top of your shortlist. Both platforms let you connect to data sources and ship custom business apps fast-but they're built for fundamentally different teams and use cases. Jet Admin is a no-code/low-code platform for app development that targets non-technical users and operations teams for building applications, while Retool is optimized for developers and technical teams who need to write JavaScript and SQL to unlock the platform's full power. This in depth comparison breaks down building approach, data connections, customization, security, deployment, and pricing so you can make a confident decision based on your team, your users, and your budget. The short answer: Choose Jet Admin if you need to ship client-facing apps, customer portals, or branded web apps without heavy engineering involvement-especially when you're serving external users at scale. Choose Retool if you have a developer-heavy team building internal tools with complex data pipelines, custom queries, and deep integrations into SQL databases and data warehouses. The single biggest differentiator: Jet Admin's drag-and-drop interface speeds up app creation for non-technical users, while Retool requires JavaScript knowledge for even simple app functions. What Is Jet Admin? Jet Admin is an AI-powered no-code/low-code platform that lets teams build secure business apps on existing data. It connects to databases, APIs, spreadsheets (like Airtable or Google Sheets), and SaaS tools, then auto-generates the interface, backend logic, and deployment pipeline. Jet Admin allows building apps quickly by connecting to databases and APIs. Its defining strengths include: Prompt-based and visual building: Jet Admin supports prompt-based app building, visual workflow automation, and a drag-and-drop interface that lets non-technical users build apps easily-no custom JavaScript required for most use cases. Customer portal and white-label focus: Jet Admin includes features for customer and partner portals with custom branding, custom domains, and branded login screens, making it ideal for client-facing apps. Auto-generated CRUD: Jet Admin automatically generates CRUD functions when connecting to databases, eliminating boilerplate coding for standard data management operations. Granular permissions and deployment flexibility: Role-based access down to rows, columns, and actions, SSO/SAML, audit logs, and both cloud and self-hosted/on-premise deployment options. Jet Admin targets non-technical users and operations teams-product managers, support leads, business ops-who need to ship apps without waiting on engineering. What Is Retool? Retool is a low-code platform designed primarily for building internal tools. Founded in June 2017 and now with over 300 employees, Retool combines drag-and-drop components with deep JavaScript and SQL scripting to give developers granular control over app logic and data. Its defining strengths include: Extensive component library: Retool offers over 100 UI components for app building, covering tables, charts, forms, modals, and more-one of the broadest selections among app builders. Developer flexibility: Retool lets technical users write queries, custom JavaScript, and SQL directly inside the platform. This makes it powerful for complex transformations and business processes. Database integrations and breadth: Retool provides over 50 native integrations with databases and APIs, including data warehouses like Snowflake, BigQuery, and Redshift, plus REST, GraphQL, and gRPC support. Governance and version control: Git integration, multi-environment support (dev/staging/prod), automated testing features (in Beta as of February 2025), and audit logs for enterprise compliance. Retool's target users are developers and engineering teams who are comfortable writing code and need complete control over internal apps. Jet Admin vs Retool: How They Compare at a Glance Factor Jet Admin Retool Best for Non-technical teams building client portals, branded apps, and internal tools Developer teams building internal tools with complex logic and data pipelines Pricing (internal users) Starts at $30/user per month Starts at $10/user per month External user pricing Unlimited external users for $39/month $8 per external user on the Pro plan Building approach Prompt-based + visual drag and drop; auto-generated CRUD Drag and drop components + JavaScript/SQL scripting Deployment options Cloud + self-hosted/on-premise (Pro and Enterprise) Cloud + self-hosted (Enterprise tier only) Learning curve Lower-accessible to non-technical users Steeper-requires JavaScript and SQL proficiency Data integrations Common SQL databases, Google Sheets, Airtable, REST/GraphQL APIs 50+ native integrations including data warehouses, NoSQL, gRPC The headline takeaway: Jet Admin optimizes for speed-to-value and external user experiences with minimal technical knowledge, while Retool optimizes for depth and developer control for internal apps. Target Audience and Building Model The way a platform lets you build apps determines who on your team can actually use it-and how fast you ship. Jet Admin offers a more accessible user interface for app building. Its prompt-based builder and visual workflow automation mean that operations teams, product managers, and support leads can connect a database and have a working admin panel or customer portal in hours, not days. Jet Admin automates CRUD actions when connecting to databases, so much of the boilerplate-forms, filters, search, export-is auto generated without writing a single line of code. For teams without dedicated developer resources, this is a major advantage in rapid development. Retool offers a visual drag-and-drop builder for app creation as well, but the similarity ends at the surface. Retool requires JavaScript knowledge for building apps-even relatively simple functions like conditional visibility, derived fields, or data transformations typically require custom JavaScript or SQL. Retool's power shows when tech savvy users need to write queries against multiple data sources, build complex state logic, or chain external API calls. But users report a steep learning curve with Retool compared to Jet Admin, and non-technical users often hit walls quickly. Winner: Jet Admin - if your team includes non technical users or you need rapid development without heavy engineering involvement. Retool wins for developer-rich teams who want full control and are comfortable with the steeper learning curve in exchange for deeper customization. Data Connections and Integrations Business apps are only as useful as the data they connect to. Both platforms support SQL databases and REST APIs for integrations, but the breadth and ease of connection differ significantly. Retool supports over 50 native integrations with databases and APIs. This includes major relational databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server), NoSQL options (MongoDB, DynamoDB, Redis), data warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, Databricks), and protocols like REST, GraphQL, and gRPC. If your stack includes multiple systems or enterprise-scale warehouses, Retool's integration catalog is hard to beat. Retool offers strong support for custom queries and enterprise integrations, making it the better choice for analytics-heavy internal tools. Jet Admin covers the most commonly needed data sources-PostgreSQL, MySQL, Firebase, Google Sheets, Airtable, REST/GraphQL APIs-and adds features like computed columns, rollups, and the ability to blend data from multiple data sources within a single view. Jet Admin allows building apps quickly by connecting to databases and APIs, and its auto-CRUD generation means you get working interfaces faster with less setup. For teams connecting to standard SaaS tools, spreadsheets, or common SQL databases, Jet Admin provides a smoother onboarding experience. Where the gap shows: if you need native connectors to third party services like Snowflake, Cosmos DB, or gRPC endpoints, Retool's breadth gives it a clear edge. If you're working with common databases and want faster time-to-value, Jet Admin excels. Winner: Retool - for maximum integration breadth, especially with data warehouses and exotic data sources. Jet Admin wins on setup speed and ease for common database integrations and SaaS tools. Customization and User Experience How much you can customize the look, feel, and behavior of your apps determines whether they feel like branded products or generic admin panels. Jet Admin provides a pixel-perfect in-app designer for custom branding. You can set custom domains, branded login screens, email templates, and fully white-labeled experiences-making it purpose-built for client portals and client-facing apps. Jet Admin also supports custom components built in React, Vue, Angular, or vanilla JS, and lets you import designs from Figma for pixel-perfect layouts. The canvas offers free-form positioning rather than a rigid grid, which gives designers more creative control. Retool uses a 12-column grid system for layout, which provides structure but constrains design freedom. Custom branding (menu themes, login pages) is available on higher plans, and you can embed custom code via JavaScript Transformers and iframes. Where Retool shines is in code extensibility: you can write custom JavaScript inline almost anywhere, chain complex SQL queries, and build advanced logic that goes beyond what visual builders typically support. For teams that need advanced customization of behavior rather than appearance, Retool's depth is unmatched. For external-facing web apps, Jet Admin feels polished out of the box-branded experiences ship without significant CSS or design work. Retool's default aesthetic is functional but clearly "internal tool first," and making it client-ready takes more effort. Winner: Jet Admin - when design polish, custom branding, and brand consistency for external users matter most. Retool wins for teams that need deep code-level control over behavior and logic through custom JavaScript. Security and Permissions Any platform handling sensitive data needs robust security and granular permissions. Both Jet Admin and Retool take this seriously, but their approaches serve different priorities. Jet Admin provides role-based access with granular permissions down to dashboards, records, data sources, and individual components. It supports SSO/SAML, enforced two-factor authentication, activity logs, and audit logs for compliance. For client portals, Jet Admin includes built-in data separation for internal and external users-meaning you can serve customer portals where each user sees only their own data without complex configuration. The on-premise deployment option uses Jet Bridge to keep data behind your VPC or VPN, adding another layer of protection. Retool offers similarly rich permission management: internal vs. external user definitions, data-level security, SSO/SAML/OpenID Connect, audit logs, and workspace isolation. Retool's enterprise plan includes more mature observability, compliance certifications (SOC2 Type II), and governance tools like source control and environment-based permissions. However, many of these features-including single sign on, advanced RBAC, and self-hosting-are gated behind the enterprise plan, which means higher cost. For external-user scenarios (customer portals, partner dashboards), Jet Admin's permission model is more accessible in lower tiers. For large enterprises in regulated industries that need proven compliance and observability at scale, Retool's enterprise security features are more mature. Winner: Close call. Jet Admin leads for accessible, out-of-the-box security for external-facing apps across all tiers. Retool leads for enterprise-grade compliance, observability, and governance-at enterprise pricing. Deployment and Hosting Options Deployment flexibility matters when IT policies restrict where data can live, or when you need to self host for regulatory or performance reasons. Jet Admin supports cloud deployment and on-premise/self-hosted deployment through its Jet Bridge agent, which can run inside your own infrastructure or VPN. Self-hosting is available in Pro and Enterprise tiers, and the platform supports multiple environments (development, staging, production). For teams that need to deploy in their own environment without vendor lock in, Jet Admin makes this accessible at a reasonable price point. Retool also supports cloud and self-hosted deployment, but recent changes have restricted self-hosting largely to the enterprise plan. Community reports from Reddit indicate that new self-hosted customers now need an enterprise agreement to enable on-premise deployment. For organizations on Team or Business plans, cloud-only deployment is the default. Both platforms support version control and environment management, but Retool's infrastructure tooling-observability integrations, performance monitoring, and capacity for large data volumes-is more battle-tested at enterprise scale. Winner: Jet Admin - for accessible self-hosting and on-premise options without requiring an enterprise-tier commitment. Retool wins on proven scale and infrastructure maturity, but only for organizations willing to pay for the enterprise plan. Pricing and Total Cost of Ownership Pricing is where Jet Admin vs Retool diverges most sharply, especially when external users enter the picture. Jet Admin pricing: Free plan available for basics Jet Admin's pricing starts at $30 per user per month for internal tools Jet Admin offers unlimited external users for $39/month on its portal-focused plan Pro tier costs $290/month for advanced features including white-labeling, custom components, and advanced integrations Enterprise: approximately $649/month+ for on-premise, dedicated support, and large-scale deployments Retool pricing: Free tier: up to 5 internal users with limited features Retool's pricing starts at $10 per user per month (Team plan) Business plan costs $50/month per standard user, unlocking audit logs, permissions, and unlimited modules Retool charges $8 per external user on the Pro plan Enterprise: custom pricing for SSO, source control, white-label, self-hosting Jet Admin and Retool both offer free plans and tiered pricing models, but the cost dynamics flip depending on your use case. For internal-only teams: Retool's $10/user/month entry point is lower than Jet Admin's $30/user/month. For small developer teams building internal tools, Retool's Team plan is more economical. For external user scenarios: Jet Admin's pricing is more economical for external user licenses compared to Retool. Building a portal for 200 external users on Jet Admin's plan costs a fixed $39/month (unlimited external users), compared to roughly 200 × $8 = $1,600/month on Retool's Pro plan. Jet Admin supports unlimited external users for a fixed price-a significant cost advantage for customer portals and partner apps. Total cost of ownership beyond licensing: Engineering time: Jet Admin reduces coding needed for common patterns, lowering developer resources required. Retool may demand more JavaScript and SQL work for equivalent results. Training: Jet Admin's lower learning curve means lower onboarding costs for non-technical teams. Scaling external users: Jet Admin's fixed-price model avoids the escalating per-user costs that Retool imposes. Winner: Jet Admin - for predictable, cost-efficient scaling, especially when serving external users. Retool wins on per-seat affordability for small, developer-only teams building purely internal apps. Jet Admin vs Retool: Which Should You Choose? Choose Jet Admin if you're building customer portals, partner dashboards, or client-facing apps where custom branding, pixel-perfect design, and serving many external users matter. It's also the right pick for teams without dedicated developers, organizations that want AI-powered no code app building, and businesses that need to self host without enterprise pricing . Jet Admin excels when rapid development and low code development need to coexist with polished user experiences. Choose Retool if your team is developer-heavy, you're building complex internal tools with deep data pipelines, and you need to write queries across multiple systems including data warehouses. Retool is the stronger choice for engineering teams that want complete control over logic, git integration for version control, and enterprise-grade compliance. It's also worth considering if you already have JavaScript and SQL expertise in-house and primarily serve internal users. For teams with mixed requirements-some internal apps, some external portals-Jet Admin provides the broader coverage without forcing you to choose between use cases. For pure internal tooling with complex logic, Retool remains a strong retool alternative to custom development. Bottom line: For most business teams evaluating both platforms today, Jet Admin delivers more value per dollar when the use case includes any external-facing component. Retool justifies its cost when deep developer flexibility and data warehouse connectivity are non-negotiable. Ready to see how Jet Admin handles your use case? Connect your data source and build your first app in minutes-no JavaScript required. Frequently Asked Questions Can I migrate from Retool to Jet Admin or vice versa? There is no automated migration path between the two platforms. Your data source connections (databases, APIs) transfer easily since they're external, but UI layouts, component logic, and workflow definitions will need to be rebuilt. Jet Admin's auto-generated CRUD and prompt-based building can accelerate reconstruction of common app patterns significantly. Which platform is better for customer-facing applications? Jet Admin is purpose-built for customer portals and client-facing apps. It includes white-labeling, custom domains, branded login screens, and unlimited external user pricing at a fixed cost. Retool can build external-facing apps, but it requires more design effort and charges per external user, which adds up quickly. Do I need developers to use either platform effectively? Jet Admin allows non-technical users to build apps easily-many features work through visual configuration and prompt-based building without writing code. Retool requires JavaScript knowledge for even simple app functions, making it less accessible for business users without technical knowledge. Which platform offers better mobile app support? Neither platform is a native mobile app builder. Both support responsive web apps and progressive web app (PWA) patterns. Retool's responsive layout works for internal dashboards on tablets. Jet Admin's pixel-perfect designer gives more control over how apps render across screen sizes, which matters more for external-facing use cases. How do these platforms compare for enterprise compliance requirements? Retool's enterprise plan offers SOC2 Type II compliance, workspace isolation, and mature observability tools for regulated industries. Jet Admin provides SSO/SAML, audit logs, granular permissions, and on-premise deployment-covering most compliance needs. For highly regulated sectors (financial services, healthcare), verify current certifications directly with each vendor. What's the typical implementation timeline for each platform? Both platforms can deliver an MVP in days to weeks. Jet Admin tends to be faster for standard admin panels and customer portals thanks to auto-generated CRUD and visual workflow automation. Retool may take longer for initial setup but offers more power for complex, logic-heavy internal tools that require custom code and multiple data sources.

title: Match Lines, Duplicate Tags, and Double-Counted Doors: Where Division 8 Takeoffs Drift
summary: Match line double counting, duplicate door tags, and repeated schedule pages skew Division 8 door counts. See where takeoffs drift and how to catch it pre-bid.
body_text: Door 132 is on the schedule but nowhere on the plans. Door 400G is on the plans but missing from the schedule. Your total can match and still be wrong. Ask a Division 8 estimator where a door count goes wrong and most will talk about counting mistakes: a missed page, a rushed pass before a deadline. But the counts that hurt on bid day mostly don’t come from miscounting. They come from the documents. Match line double counting, duplicate door tags, and schedule pages that repeat across buildings quietly put doors into a takeoff twice, or drop them out entirely, before the estimator makes a single mistake. The math is unforgiving at commercial scale. Even a 99% accurate count on a 2,000-door project leaves 20 doors wrong. And the bad end of this is real: one estimating team missed roughly 200 doors on a Denver job because a schedule was buried in the set, and lost the job over it. This piece names the five places Division 8 counts drift and how to catch each one before the number goes out. How Match Line Double Counting Happens on Sectional Plans On a large footprint, the architect splits each floor plan into sections (area A, area B, area C) with match lines marking the seams between sheets. A door that sits on or near a seam gets drawn on both sheets. Count sheet by sheet, the way every takeoff naturally proceeds, and that opening lands in the count twice. One door in the building, two doors in the bid. Match line double counting is worst on exactly the sets where review time is scarcest: big education and healthcare footprints, sectional sheets, addendum churn. And the direction of the error matters. A double-counted door pads your material number and prices you out; a door lost between sections eats your margin after award. Match lines can hand you either one. The mechanism in one sentence: sectional plans show the same door twice by design, and any count that proceeds sheet by sheet will double it unless a person or a tool is deduplicating across the seams. Duplicate Tags and Reused Codes in the Schedule The schedule itself carries the second trap. In one 752-door commercial schedule, a single door tag, S60004A, appeared three times. Architects also reuse type codes across the multiple schedules in one set, which is how you end up with a door listed as hollow metal in the schedule while the elevation clearly shows a storefront aluminum door: the code was recycled from another part of the schedule. Estimators trade these stories constantly. One on r/estimators: “I saw a Div 08 one recently where there were 3 different clear openings for one door on the same page.” A tag is not an opening. Treating the schedule as ground truth is how tag problems become count problems: the same document failure we broke down in the fake door schedule problem , where the schedule is really just a tag and it’s the estimator’s job to find every opening that carries it. What to take from this: duplicate and recycled tags mean the schedule can’t be trusted as a count of openings. It’s an index into the plans, and the count has to survive a reconciliation between the two. Repeated Schedules and Unit Math in Multifamily Multifamily and student housing sets multiply everything. The same unit type repeats across floors and buildings, and schedule pages often repeat per building, with Building C carrying what is effectively Building A’s schedule. Count a repeated page fresh each time and an entire building’s doors go in twice. Miss that the pages differ in one line (one unit type swapped, one hardware set changed) and the shortcut fails the other way. Unit math compounds it. A patio door that appears on the schedule but not on the unit plan (or the reverse) looks like a one-door discrepancy until you multiply it by forty units across three buildings. In repetitive product types, every small document error ships at scale. The rule for repetitive sets: verify whether repeated schedule pages are actually identical before counting them as copies, and resolve unit-type discrepancies before multiplying them. When the Schedule and the Plans Disagree The remaining traps are the flat disagreements. A door sits in the schedule and never appears on any plan. A door sits on the plans, assigned to a hardware set and clearly real, and is missing from every schedule. A door appears three times in the schedule and eight times on the floor plans. Each one is a count drift waiting to happen, and each one is also an RFI: the first estimator to submit RFIs is the first one to get answers. The discipline that catches them is reconciliation in both directions: every scheduled door found on the plans, every planned door found in the schedule, every mismatch either resolved or documented. And keep the record. When the GC challenges your number, the log of what you found and how you resolved it (this door assigned to the set from the spec, that duplicate accepted as one opening) is what lets you defend the count instead of re-arguing it. That review-and-record side of the workflow has its own piece: how Division 8 estimators review AI takeoffs and keep the sign-off . Reconcile both directions, resolve or document every mismatch, and keep the audit trail. That’s the whole discipline, and it’s the difference between a count you have and a count you can defend. Why General-Purpose Takeoff Tools Don’t Catch the Drift General-purpose takeoff tools count what’s drawn. That’s their scope, and inside it they’re fine. But estimators who run them on Division 8 work report the familiar artifacts: doorways double-lined so the same opening calculates twice, measurements picked up behind cabinets, and door categories still built and tagged manually, unit by unit, in a tool that was supposed to automate the tagging. The deeper issue isn’t the artifacts. It’s that every trap in this article lives between documents: a seam between two sheets, a tag shared by two schedules, a schedule page shared by two buildings. A general counting engine has no concept of a match line, a reused tag, or a repeated schedule. Counting doors is mechanical. Catching the same door twice across a match line is reconciliation, and reconciliation is where general-purpose tools stop. In short: the counting layer was never the hard part of a Division 8 takeoff. The cross-document layer is, and it’s the layer generic tools don’t see. A Pre-Bid Checklist for a Count You Can Defend Before a Division 8 number goes out, six checks catch nearly all of the drift: Reconcile the schedule count against the plan count, in both directions, area by area. Scan for duplicate tags within each schedule and reused codes across schedules in the same set. On sectional sets, walk the match lines specifically; every door near a seam gets one deliberate look. On multifamily, confirm repeated schedule pages are actually identical before treating any building as a copy. Count leaves separately from doors; pairs and multi-leaf openings drift independently of door counts. Log every resolution, and turn the unresolved ones into RFIs the day the invitation arrives. Done by hand, that review is real hours, and it’s a second pass over work you’ve already done. The economics only change when review gets targeted: check the handful of openings where something disagrees instead of re-checking all of them. On that 752-door schedule, the difference was reviewing the three or four flagged problems instead of the full set. That’s the design behind Fresco’s approach to Division 8 review. It reads the schedule, the plans, and the spec together, deduplicates doors across match lines automatically, flags duplicate tags and schedule-plan mismatches, and hands the estimator the exceptions: the puzzle mostly assembled, with the handful of non-conforming pieces called out. Every resolution is logged, so the audit trail behind the bid builds itself. That trade is steepest for the shops with the least review time, and nobody has less of it than the solo Division 8 estimator turning away winnable bids . It’s what turns the checklist above from an afternoon into minutes. The checklist answer in one line: reconcile both directions, hunt duplicates, walk the seams, verify repeats, count leaves, and log everything. Then let flagged exceptions, not full re-counts, absorb your review time. When This Advice Doesn’t Apply A 30-door tenant improvement on a single plan sheet has no match lines and no repeated schedules. Count it, reconcile it against the schedule once, and move on. If you’re a distributor quoting off a supplied door schedule alone, with no plans in hand, full reconciliation isn’t in your scope. Say so on the quote, and qualify that the count reflects the schedule as issued. Everywhere else (sectional sets, repetitive product types, multi-schedule documents) assume the drift is in the set until reconciliation proves otherwise. Frequently Asked Questions How accurate does a door takeoff need to be to bid from? For material counts, the working standard is exact, not close. Division 8 material quotes don’t carry the buffer to absorb count errors, and the percentages hide the stakes: 99% accuracy on a 2,000-door project still means 20 wrong doors. The practical target isn’t a percentage. It’s a reconciled count, where every schedule-plan mismatch has been resolved or documented before pricing. How do I check a door takeoff for double counting before the bid goes out? Reconcile the schedule count against the plan count in both directions, then walk the specific trap locations: seams where match line double counting happens on sectional sets, duplicate tags within and across schedules, and repeated schedule pages in multifamily. Check leaf counts separately from door counts. Anything that disagrees gets resolved, documented, or turned into an RFI, never silently absorbed. Why doesn’t my door count match the door schedule? Usually because the schedule was never a complete count of openings. Door schedules carry duplicate tags, recycled codes, and doors that exist on the plans but never made the schedule, and the reverse. On commercial work, treat the schedule as an index to verify against the plans, not as ground truth, and expect the reconciliation to surface a handful of legitimate discrepancies on any real set. Do AI takeoff tools double count doors? General-purpose counting tools can: estimators report doorways double-lined so one opening calculates twice, and measurements picked up behind cabinets. Division 8-specific tools handle the drift differently: Fresco deduplicates doors that appear across match lines automatically, flags duplicate tags and schedule-plan mismatches, and presents the exceptions for the estimator to resolve, so the double-count is caught in review instead of discovered after award. Key Takeaways Door counts mostly drift in the documents, not in the counting: match line double counting, duplicate tags, repeated schedule pages, and schedule-plan mismatches put doors in twice or drop them entirely. A double-counted door prices you out of the job; a missed door eats the margin after award. The traps hand you both. Even 99% accuracy leaves 20 wrong doors on a 2,000-door project. Reconciliation in both directions is how you find out which 20. General-purpose tools count what’s drawn; every trap in this piece lives between documents. Review exceptions, not everything: a flagged list of three or four problem openings beats a second pass over 752 doors. If your next set is sectional, repetitive, or carrying more schedules than it should, upload it to Fresco and see what the cross-document flags find before the number goes out. title: Clearlake Capital and the Shift Toward AI-Native Investing
summary: AI platform for Private Equity diligence — aggregate deal data, deploy custom AI workflows, and transform fund knowledge into proprietary intelligence.
body_text: Every private equity firm today has access to the same frontier models. The reasoning layer is no longer the moat. It's the floor. The question isn't whether a firm uses AI. It's what the firm is building underneath it. That question is shaping how firms think about their AI strategy. Some firms are AI-assisted , applying models to existing processes to make familiar work faster. The deal flow, the diligence, the IC all look the same, with a faster engine attached. Other firms are building toward AI-native : rethinking what the firm sees, how it reasons, and what it remembers, with infrastructure underneath the models that makes the firm's own intelligence compound. Clearlake’s experience offers a useful lens into a broader shift underway across private equity. As firms move beyond experimenting with AI tools, a growing number are asking a different question: how can institutional knowledge itself become a scalable asset? Clearlake's Architectural Bet Clearlake is a leading global investment firm with more than $185 billion in assets under management across private equity, credit, and related strategies. Through Pathway Capital Management, a division of Clearlake, the firm offers a comprehensive markets platform spanning private equity, credit, secondaries, co-investments and infrastructure. Known for its operationally focused investment approach, Clearlake has long viewed technology, data, and AI as strategic enablers of value creation – both within its investment platform and across its portfolio companies. Like many leading investment firms, Clearlake initially approached AI through internal experimentation. Over time, the firm reached a conclusion that many organizations are now arriving at: the long-term opportunity is not simply deploying models, but building the infrastructure that allows institutional knowledge, investment frameworks, and accumulated experience to become more accessible and reusable . We sought a partner who understood our business and our ambition to differentiate through data. Building a scaled platform required specialized expertise, and we wanted to do it alongside a team whose core focus was turning data into a strategic advantage. The result was a true partnership that helped accelerate our vision. — Tony La Rosa, Managing Director, Technology and O.P.S.®, Clearlake Capital 1) Scaling institutional judgment One of the most significant opportunities AI creates for investment organizations is the ability to make institutional judgment more consistent and accessible. Firms develop pattern recognition over decades, but much of that knowledge traditionally resides in documents, conversations, and individual experiences. At Clearlake, that has meant translating elements of the firm’s investment and value creation approach into structured frameworks that can be referenced and refined over time. 2) Making institutional memory actionable When a new opportunity comes to market, every PE firm faces the same starting point. The information that matters often exists somewhere inside the firm. Getting to it takes time. Firms are increasingly looking for ways to change that starting point. Clearlake’s approach focuses on making relevant prior investment analysis, expertise, evaluations, operating insights, and adjacent learnings easier to access at the beginning of an investment process rather than after extensive searching. Deal team can access their firm's context graph across multiple layers: That asset compounds. The 10th opportunity in a sub-sector benefits from 9 prior looks, and the work the deal team starts isn't searching. It's deciding. 3) Conviction over orientation IC can be the most consequential meeting at any private equity firm. It's where conviction gets tested, where dissent gets aired, and where capital gets committed. The quality of that meeting depends on what the committee can spend its time on. The broader objective is not simply efficiency. It is creating more space for higher-value discussions and decision making. At Clearlake, that means bringing together information, diligence, selective sector experience, historical context, and relevant insights into a more unified view. 4) Knowledge as a compounding asset The most interesting aspect of AI-native investing may not be productivity gains. It may be the ability to compound organizational learning over time. Clearlake’s deep investment and operating experience suggests that when knowledge is captured, structured, and made retrievable, each investment process can contribute to the next. The result is knowledge that grows more valuable as the organization gains experience. What Doesn't Commoditize Foundation models are the same for everyone. The reasoning layer is where capability gets distributed. It's not where advantage gets built. A great model can read a CIM. It can produce a clean analysis on any deal in any sector. What it cannot do is know what a specific firm has seen before. It cannot tell a deal team that the firm looked at this exact sub-sector eighteen months ago, or that a comparable business model in the portfolio grew EBITDA 40% with a specific operational playbook. That context isn't in the model. It can only be built by the firm. This is increasingly where firms are focusing their efforts. While foundation models continue to improve and become more widely available, institutional knowledge remains unique to each organization. Clearlake’s approach reflects a broader belief that durable advantage will come less from access to AI itself and more from how firms capture, structure, and apply their own accumulated experience. We believe that in five years, the firms that started building this asset in 2026 will be operating in a different category. We chose to be one of them. — Tony La Rosa, Managing Director, Technology and O.P.S.®, Clearlake Capital The firms making this choice now are accumulating a year of compounding that their competitors may not be able to replicate. The gap that opens up isn't a tooling gap. It's a knowledge gap. And knowledge gaps don't close by buying software. The Firms Defining What's Next The private equity industry appears to be approaching a fork in the road. One path uses AI primarily to accelerate existing workflows. The other uses AI to make institutional knowledge more scalable, accessible, and durable. Clearlake’s experience suggests that the distinction matters. While models may become more increasingly commoditized, the knowledge, judgement, and experience accumulated within a firm remain unique. The firms that successfully combine those assets with AL may not simply work faster. They may develop institutional intelligence that compounds over time, creating advantages that become meaningful with every investment, every operating initiative, and every decision. In that sense, the question is no longer whether AI will reshape private equity. The question is which firms will use it to build something that lasts.

title: COVID-19: Pandemic Leads to a Huge Increase in Email Phishing Attempts
summary: Safety Insurance is a premier provider of auto, home, and business owners insurance in Massachusetts, Maine, and New Hampshire.
body_text: Cyber-criminals are using the current Covid-19 pandemic to help with their phishing scams. We encourage everyone to be extra vigilant when opening emails and clicking links within them. Some helpful hints: Don’t be taken in by the sender’s name. Scammers can put any name they like in the “from” field. Look out for spelling and grammatical errors. Not all crooks make mistakes, but many do. Take extra time to review messages for telltale signs that they’re fraudulent. Check the URL before you type it in or click a link. If the website you land on doesn’t look right, steer clear. Never enter data that a website shouldn’t be asking for. A site that’s open to the public, such as the CDC or WHO, will never ask for your login credentials. If you realize you just revealed your password to impostors, change it as soon as possible. The crooks try to use stolen passwords immediately, so the sooner you change your password, the more likely you are to stop them for doing anything malicious. At first glance, the sender’s email address appears to be legitimate, for example cdc-gov.org or cdcgov.org. The criminals create domains that are very close to the real CDC site — cdc.gov. Even though the link looks like it will take you to a CDC.gov website about the Corona virus, it will not. More than likely, you will land on a fake Microsoft Outlook login page, created by criminals to steal user names and passwords, which they control. There is no reason to provide login credentials to visit a public website, such as the CDC.

title: What California’s ADDE Menu Act Means for Restaurants and Food Trucks of Different Sizes - The Avocado - Avocado POS
summary: California’s new Allergen Disclosure for Dining Experiences (ADDE) Menu Act, signed into law in October 2025, is the first of its kind in the U.S. to require written allergen information on menus.
body_text: Who must comply, who’s exempt, and why small operators should still pay attention. A Big Law with a Targeted Reach California’s new Allergen Disclosure for Dining Experiences (ADDE) Menu Act , signed into law in October 2025, is the first of its kind in the U.S. to require written allergen information on menus . But while the headlines make it sound like every restaurant and food truck will have to overhaul their menus, the truth is more nuanced. The ADDE Menu Act’s requirements depend heavily on the size and scope of your business . Here’s a breakdown of who’s affected — and why even exempt businesses should start paying attention now. ⚖️ Who Must Comply The law applies to restaurants and food service businesses with 20 or more locations nationwide that operate under the same name and branding . That means: Chain restaurants such as McDonald’s, Panera, or Shake Shack Franchise groups that share a brand and standardized menu Multi-unit restaurant companies with centralized management Food truck brands that have 20 or more trucks operating under the same name If your operation falls into this category, you’ll need to: Disclose in writing which of the “Top 9” allergens are present in each menu item (milk, eggs, fish, shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soy, sesame). Display this information on printed menus or through digital access (like a QR code). Provide a printed option for customers who can’t use digital devices. Keep information current whenever recipes or suppliers change. Train staff to understand and communicate allergen information clearly. The compliance deadline is July 1, 2026 , and enforcement will come through the California Department of Public Health and local health agencies. 🚫 Who Is Exempt (for Now) The ADDE Menu Act does not apply to small, independent, or local food service businesses. That includes: Independent restaurants with fewer than 20 locations Local chains that don’t meet the national threshold Single-location food trucks or small local fleets So, a mom-and-pop diner, a single taco truck, or a small three-location café chain does not have to comply with the new labeling requirements. This exemption was a deliberate choice. Lawmakers limited the scope to large chains after small business advocates and the California Restaurant Association argued that smaller operators would struggle with the administrative and technical burden of constant allergen documentation. 💡 Why Small Operators Should Still Care Even though you may not have to comply, here’s why it’s smart to start preparing anyway: 1. Consumer Expectations Are Changing Customers increasingly expect transparency about ingredients and allergens. Many families with food allergies already prefer chains precisely because they can access clear allergen data. By offering your own allergen list — even voluntarily — you can stand out as a trusted local option for these customers. 2. It’s Likely a Preview of What’s Coming California often leads the nation in restaurant regulation. Once the ADDE Menu Act is fully implemented, other states — or even local cities — could expand similar requirements to smaller operations. Getting ahead of that curve now can save headaches later. 3. Operational Benefits Tracking allergens means documenting ingredients, standardizing recipes, and training staff — all of which improve food safety, consistency, and customer confidence. For food trucks especially, where menu changes are frequent, a clear ingredient tracking process can make daily operations smoother and reduce costly errors. 📋 Practical Steps for All Operators Whether you’re a major chain or a one-truck start-up, here are steps you can take to prepare or voluntarily align with best practices: Create a simple allergen chart listing menu items and which of the Top 9 allergens they contain. Audit suppliers to ensure you have up-to-date ingredient information. Train your team to respond accurately to allergen inquiries — “I’ll check” is better than guessing. Consider digital menus or QR codes for easy updates and transparency. Market your transparency — diners appreciate restaurants that care about their safety. 🕒 Timeline and Next Steps Now–Spring 2026: Large operators begin auditing ingredients and updating menu systems. By July 1, 2026: All covered chains (20+ locations) must have allergen disclosures in place. Beyond 2026: Other states — or California cities — may explore similar rules for smaller businesses. Small operators won’t be required to make changes immediately, but being proactive now can save costs later and build stronger customer relationships today. The Bottom Line The ADDE Menu Act is aimed squarely at large, multi-location chains — not independent restaurants or single food trucks. But its ripple effects will touch everyone in the food industry. Customers are already learning to look for allergen transparency, and sooner or later, those expectations will extend to every menu. So even if you’re not required to comply yet, now’s the time to think about how your business can communicate safety and trust — whether that’s through a printed allergen guide, a digital menu, or simply better staff training. Transparency is no longer just a regulatory issue — it’s good business.
